plan.title: A lesson-only reply: a follow-up about how it went, tied to the lesson

context.text: Tonight, Riley: 7 pm at your desk, 15 minutes. Read the discovery-call article and write one opening question for a gym owner. Send a screenshot or a quick voice note when it's done.

transcript.text: [voice: Done. I learned discovery calls should start with their problem, not my pitch. I wrote my question: what's the hardest part of keeping members past month two?]

Nice work, Riley! Day 3 is done, and "what's the hardest part of keeping members past month two?" is a strong opener. It starts with their problem, just like you said it should. 🔥 How did this one feel? Was it easy to write, or did you have to work to keep the pitch out of it?
honestly it felt kind of awkward writing it, like I was guessing what they'd say

That awkward feeling is normal, Riley. You're writing for someone you haven't talked to yet. What do you think would make it feel less like guessing: hearing a real gym owner's answer, or having a few more questions ready?
yeah I think talking to an actual owner would help

That's a real insight, Riley. Guessing is what a first draft feels like, and hearing a real owner's answer is what fixes it. So tomorrow we move toward that conversation:

• Tue at 7 pm, at your desk, 15 min
• Pick the gym owner you know best from your two gyms
• Write a 2-3 line message asking for a 10-minute chat about keeping members past month two
• Send it if you're ready, then send me a voice note reading it out

Work for you?
Locked in, Riley. Tomorrow at 7 pm you're one step closer to a real owner's answer, and that's how you stop guessing. Talk then. 💪

Warm and sincere, no overfamiliarity or emoji.

Warm and specific, but calmer than pushy-level energy; no emoji or affection issues.

Brief, warm, one flexing emoji as punctuation.

Follow-ups tie to Riley's words ('awkward', 'guessing'), but the first text asks two questions, against one per text.

Counts the voice note, praises the lesson specifically, asks one awkwardness question, proposes a fully defined desk 7 pm 15-min step, and confirms after 'sounds good' without a new question; the first text's double question is the flaw.

grade.summary: ZOH handled the regression well: it counted the proof, celebrated the lesson, followed up on the awkwardness, and proposed a fully defined next step that used Riley's words before asking for agreement. The main misses were the first text running long with two questions, and the proposal missing a reason and alternative for its proof and not reusing the earlier lesson.
